title: Chemical energetics
objectives: Understand that chemical reactions are accompanied by enthalpy changes, which can be exothermic (ΔH negative) or endothermic (ΔH positive)
Construct and interpret reaction pathway diagrams, in terms of the enthalpy change of reaction and the activation energy
Define and use standard conditions and the enthalpy changes of reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation
Understand that energy transfers occur during chemical reactions because of the breaking and making of chemical bonds
Use bond energies (ΔH positive, bond breaking) to calculate enthalpy changes, and understand why average bond energies give approximate values
Calculate enthalpy changes from experimental results using q = mcΔT
Apply Hess’s law to construct simple energy cycles and carry out calculations, including with ΔH<sub>f</sub>, ΔH<sub>c</sub> and bond energy data
why: Every fuel, battery, food label and industrial process depends on energy changes. In this chapter you learn to measure energy changes in the lab and to calculate the ones you cannot measure directly. Hess’s law calculations appear on almost every Paper 1 and Paper 2, and the ideas return in equilibria, kinetics and the A Level energetics topics.
intro: When bonds break, energy is taken in; when bonds form, energy is released. The difference is the enthalpy change, ΔH. You will meet the standard enthalpy changes you must define, measure ΔH with simple calorimetry, and use Hess’s law to combine known values into unknown ones.

blocks.h: Reaction pathway diagrams
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.

A reaction pathway (energy profile) diagram plots energy against the progress of reaction. Draw ΔH as an arrow from the reactant level to the product level (down for exothermic, up for endothermic). Draw E<sub>a</sub> from the reactant level to the top of the hump.

blocks.name: profile
blocks.title: Energy profile builder
blocks.h: Use the sliders to set ΔH and E<sub>a</sub>. The diagram redraws with labelled arrows. Switch on a catalyst to see the lower-energy route, and read off the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
E<sub>a</sub>(reverse) = E<sub>a</sub>(forward) − ΔH. For an exothermic reaction this is bigger than the forward E<sub>a</sub>.
Why are there energy changes?

Breaking a bond always takes in energy (endothermic). Making a bond always releases energy (exothermic). If the new bonds in the products are stronger overall than the bonds broken in the reactants, more energy is released than taken in, and the reaction is exothermic.

blocks.wrong: Burning fuel releases energy because bonds in the fuel break.
blocks.right: Bond breaking needs energy. The energy comes out when the very strong bonds in CO₂ and H₂O form.

blocks.q: A reaction has ΔH = −90 kJ mol⁻¹ and E<sub>a</sub> = +120 kJ mol⁻¹. What is E<sub>a</sub> for the reverse reaction?
blocks.why: From the products (90 below the reactants) up to the peak (120 above the reactants) is 90 + 120 = 210 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.h: Standard conditions: 298 K (25 °C) and 101 kPa, with every substance in its standard state (its normal physical state under these conditions). A standard value is shown with the symbol ⦵, as in ΔH⦵.

blocks.term: Standard enthalpy change of reaction, ΔH<sub>r</sub><sup>⦵</sup>
blocks.h: The enthalpy change when the amounts of reactants shown in the equation react to give products under standard conditions.

blocks.term: Standard enthalpy change of formation, ΔH<sub>f</sub><sup>⦵</sup>
blocks.h: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions, all substances in their standard states.

blocks.term: Standard enthalpy change of combustion, ΔH<sub>c</sub><sup>⦵</sup>
blocks.h: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in an excess of oxygen under standard conditions.

blocks.term: Standard enthalpy change of neutralisation, ΔH<sub>neut</sub><sup>⦵</sup>
blocks.h: The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with a base under standard conditions.
ΔHf of any element in its standard state is zero. Fractions such as ½O₂ are fine on the left of a formation or combustion equation; the 1 mol rule applies to the substance being formed or burned.

items: ΔH<sub>f</sub> of O₂(g) is zero.
It is an element in its standard state.
The equation C(g) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g) represents ΔH<sub>f</sub> of methane.
Carbon’s standard state is C(s), graphite.
ΔH<sub>c</sub> of hydrogen is the same as ΔH<sub>f</sub> of liquid water.
Both are H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l).
Standard conditions are 298 °C and 101 kPa.
The temperature is 298 K (25 °C).

blocks.h: q = mcΔT

items: q: heat energy transferred to (or from) the water or solution, in J
m: mass of water or solution heated, in g (for dilute solutions, 1 cm³ ≈ 1 g; use the total volume after mixing)
c: specific heat capacity, 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water
ΔT: temperature change, in K (a change of 1 °C = a change of 1 K)

blocks.h: ΔH = −q / n

Divide by the number of moles, n, of the substance named in the definition (the fuel burned, the limiting reactant, or the water formed). The minus sign is there because a temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic. Convert J to kJ.

blocks.q: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. The temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Calculate ΔH<sub>neut</sub>.
blocks.err: Using 50 g instead of the total 100 g of solution halves the answer.

blocks.q: Burning 0.25 g of methanol (M<sub>r</sub> 32) raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 12.0 °C. Calculate ΔH<sub>c</sub>.
blocks.err: Putting the mass of fuel into q = mcΔT. m is the mass of the water that is heated.

blocks.h: Why experimental values are smaller than data-book values

items: heat lost to the surroundings (air, the beaker, the thermometer)
incomplete combustion of the fuel (soot, CO)
evaporation of the fuel or water
heat capacity of the container ignored

blocks.h: If only a percentage of the heat reaches the water, divide the heat the water gained by that fraction to get the heat the reaction released.
The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same.
Hess’s law lets you calculate ΔH for reactions that are hard to measure directly (too slow, unwanted side products, or impossible to do cleanly) by going round an energy cycle.

Round the cycle: ΣΔHf(reactants) + ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products). Going against an arrow, change its sign.

blocks.h: Combining equations
You can also add and subtract whole thermochemical equations: reverse an equation → change the sign of ΔH; multiply an equation → multiply ΔH by the same number.

blocks.q: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) ΔH = −393.5; CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) ΔH = −283.0. Find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g).
blocks.a: Keep the first, reverse the second: −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹. (This reaction cannot be measured directly because some CO₂ always forms.)

blocks.h: The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state.
ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)

Draw out the displayed formulae, count every bond broken in the reactants and every bond made in the products, and use the formula. Bonds that are the same on both sides can be left out, as long as you leave them out of both sums.

blocks.q: Calculate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–H 413, O=O 496, C=O 805, O–H 463.
blocks.err: Writing formed − broken gives +818, the wrong sign.

blocks.h: Why bond-energy answers are approximate

items: Data-book values are average bond energies, taken over many different compounds; the real strength of a bond depends on its environment.
Bond energies refer to the gaseous state. If a reactant or product is a liquid or solid (such as H₂O(l)), the enthalpy of the change of state is not included.

blocks.q: Drag into order of increasing bond energy (weakest first):
items: Cl–Cl (242)

summary: Exothermic: ΔH negative, energy released to the surroundings. Endothermic: ΔH positive, energy taken in.
Activation energy: the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. On a pathway diagram E<sub>a</sub> is measured from the reactants to the peak.
Standard conditions: 298 K and 101 kPa, substances in their standard states.
ΔH<sub>f</sub>: 1 mol of compound from its elements. ΔH<sub>c</sub>: 1 mol of substance burned completely in excess oxygen. ΔH<sub>neut</sub>: 1 mol of water formed from acid and base.
ΔH<sub>f</sub> of an element in its standard state is zero.
Bond breaking is endothermic; bond making is exothermic.
q = mcΔT (m = mass of water/solution heated); ΔH = −q/n.
Experimental ΔH<sub>c</sub> is less exothermic than the data-book value because of heat losses and incomplete combustion.
Hess’s law: ΔH is independent of the route.
With ΔH<sub>f</sub> data: ΔH = Σproducts − Σreactants. With ΔH<sub>c</sub> data: ΔH = Σreactants − Σproducts.
With bond energies: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Average bond energies give approximate answers and apply to gases.

practice.q: Write the equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of calcium carbonate.

assessment_s.q:
A student finds ΔHc of butan-1-ol (Mr 74.0). 0.370 g of the fuel heats 100 g of water from 19.5 °C to 37.0 °C.
(a) Calculate the heat transferred to the water. [1]
(b) Calculate ΔHc in kJ mol⁻¹. [2]
(c) The data-book value is −2676 kJ mol⁻¹. Give two reasons for the difference. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) q = 100 × 4.18 × 17.5 = 7315 J
(b) n = 0.370/74.0 = 0.00500 mol; ΔHc = −7.315/0.00500 = −1463 kJ mol⁻¹
(c) heat lost to the surroundings (and the can); incomplete combustion; evaporation of the alcohol

assessment_s.q:
Use the data to answer the questions. ΔHf / kJ mol⁻¹: NO(g) +90.3, NO₂(g) +33.2. Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: N≡N 944, O=O 496.
(a) Define standard enthalpy change of formation. [2]
(b) Calculate ΔH for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g). [2]
(c) Use the bond energies and ΔHf(NO) to estimate the N=O bond energy in NO. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements; under standard conditions (298 K, 101 kPa) in standard states
(b) 2(33.2) − 2(90.3) = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹
(c) ½N≡N + ½O=O → N=O: 90.3 = (472 + 248) − E, so E = 629.7 ≈ 630 kJ mol⁻¹

pp.skill: Signs of enthalpy changes for physical and chemical processes
pp.mis: Thinking any change of state releases energy
pp.stem:
Three processes are listed.
1 H₂O(l) → H₂O(g)
2 Mg(s) + ½O₂(g) → MgO(s)
3 Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
Which processes have a positive enthalpy change?
pp.exp: 1: boiling overcomes intermolecular forces, so energy is taken in (+). 3: ionisation always needs energy (+). 2: burning magnesium releases a lot of energy (−).

pp.skill: Recognising an exothermic reaction and whether it is redox
pp.mis: Assuming every reaction that gives out heat is a redox reaction
pp.stem: A self-heating drinks can works by letting water reach calcium oxide: CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(s). The can gets hot. Which statement describes this reaction?
opts: It is endothermic and calcium is oxidised.
It is exothermic and calcium is oxidised.
It is exothermic and no element changes oxidation number.
It is endothermic and no element changes oxidation number.
pp.exp: The surroundings get hotter, so energy is released: exothermic. Ca is +2, O is −2 and H is +1 on both sides, so this is not a redox reaction.

pp.skill: Deducing what a positive ΔH value tells you
pp.mis: Treating any ΔH as an enthalpy of formation
pp.stem:
N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g) ΔH = +58 kJ mol⁻¹
Which deduction can be made from this information?
opts: The standard enthalpy change of formation of NO₂ is +29 kJ mol⁻¹.
The reaction absorbs energy from the surroundings.
Two moles of NO₂ have less energy than one mole of N₂O₄.
The reaction cannot take place at room temperature.
pp.exp: A positive ΔH means the reaction is endothermic: it takes in energy, so the products (2NO₂) are at a higher enthalpy than N₂O₄. ΔH<sub>f</sub> must start from the elements N₂ and O₂, so +29 is not ΔH<sub>f</sub>(NO₂). Endothermic reactions can still happen at room temperature.

pp.skill: Bond breaking and bond making in terms of energy
pp.mis: Thinking that breaking bonds releases energy
pp.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on strong heating: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement explains why this reaction is endothermic?
opts: More energy is released in breaking bonds than is taken in when bonds form.
More energy is taken in to break bonds than is released when new bonds form.
pp.exp: Breaking bonds always needs energy; forming bonds always releases energy. If more is taken in than given out, the overall change is endothermic.

pp.skill: Total bond energies of reactants and products
pp.mis: Getting the sign the wrong way round
pp.stem: A reaction in which every reactant and product is a gas is endothermic. Which statement about this reaction is correct?
opts: The total bond energy of the reactants is greater than that of the products, and ΔH is positive.
The total bond energy of the reactants is less than that of the products, and ΔH is positive.
The total bond energy of the reactants is greater than that of the products, and ΔH is negative.
The total bond energy of the reactants is less than that of the products, and ΔH is negative.
pp.exp: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). For ΔH to be positive, more energy is needed to break the reactant bonds than is released by forming the product bonds.

pp.skill: Enthalpy changes of melting and boiling
pp.mis: Thinking covalent bonds break when a molecular liquid boils
pp.stem:
Ethanol melts at −114 °C and boils at 78 °C. Three statements about the enthalpy changes of melting, ΔHm, and of vaporisation, ΔHvap, of ethanol are given.
1 Both ΔHm and ΔHvap are positive.
2 ΔHvap is larger than ΔHm.
3 C–H and O–H covalent bonds are broken when ethanol boils.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: Melting and boiling both take in energy (1 true). Boiling separates the molecules completely, so far more intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) are overcome than when melting (2 true). No covalent bonds inside the molecules break (3 false).

pp.skill: Standard conditions for enthalpy changes
pp.mis: Writing 298 °C instead of 298 K
pp.stem:
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) ΔH⦵ = −196 kJ mol⁻¹
Which statement about this value is correct?
opts: It is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of SO₂ reacts.
It refers to a temperature of 298 K and a pressure of 101 kPa.
It is the standard enthalpy change of formation of SO₃.
pp.exp: Standard conditions are 298 K and 101 kPa (with substances in their standard states). The value is for the equation as written: 2 mol SO₂ reacting. It is not ΔH<sub>f</sub>, which starts from elements and forms 1 mol of product.

pp.skill: Writing the equation for an enthalpy of formation
pp.mis: Using gaseous atoms instead of elements in their standard states
pp.stem: ΔH<sub>f</sub><sup>⦵</sup> of ethane, C₂H₆(g), is −84.7 kJ mol⁻¹. To which equation does this value apply?
pp.exp: ΔH<sub>f</sub>: 1 mol of compound formed from its elements in their standard states. Carbon is C(s) (graphite) and hydrogen is H₂(g). D forms 2 mol.

pp.skill: Enthalpy of formation equation for an ionic oxide
pp.mis: Forming more or less than one mole of product
pp.stem: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of aluminium oxide?
pp.exp: Exactly 1 mol of Al₂O₃ must form, from Al(s) and O₂(g). Fractions are allowed on the left-hand side.

pp.skill: States in an enthalpy of formation equation
pp.mis: Choosing the wrong physical state for the product
pp.stem: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of methanol?
pp.exp: Methanol is a liquid at 298 K and 101 kPa, so its standard state is (l). The elements must be in their standard states: C(s), H₂(g), O₂(g).

pp.skill: Recognising which reaction is a formation reaction
pp.mis: Missing that a reactant is a compound or not in its standard state
pp.stem: Only one of these equations describes a formation reaction. Which one?
pp.exp: Only B forms one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states. A starts from a compound (CO); C forms 2 mol; D uses Na(g), but sodium’s standard state is Na(s).

pp.skill: Interpreting a reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction
pp.mis: Drawing the activation energy from the products
pp.stem: For an endothermic reaction with activation energy E<sub>a</sub>, which description of its reaction pathway diagram is correct?
opts: The products are below the reactants, and E<sub>a</sub> is measured from the products to the peak.
The products are above the reactants, and E<sub>a</sub> is measured from the reactants to the peak.
The products are above the reactants, and E<sub>a</sub> is smaller than ΔH.
The products are below the reactants, and E<sub>a</sub> is measured from the reactants to the peak.
pp.exp: Endothermic: the products are higher in energy than the reactants. E<sub>a</sub> is always measured from the reactants up to the top of the barrier, so for an endothermic reaction E<sub>a</sub> must be at least as large as ΔH.

pp.skill: Relating E<sub>a</sub> of forward and reverse reactions to ΔH
pp.mis: Subtracting instead of adding
pp.stem: A reaction has ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹ and an activation energy of +60 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
pp.exp: The peak is 60 kJ above the reactants, and the products are 40 kJ below the reactants. From the products, the climb to the peak is 60 + 40 = 100 kJ mol⁻¹.

pp.skill: Choosing the enthalpy profile for given ΔH and E<sub>a</sub>
pp.mis: Ignoring the relative sizes of E<sub>a</sub> and ΔH
pp.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +45 kJ mol⁻¹ and E<sub>a</sub> = +50 kJ mol⁻¹. Which description of its enthalpy profile is correct?
opts: The products are 45 kJ mol⁻¹ below the reactants; the peak is 50 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants.
The products are 45 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants; the peak is only 5 kJ mol⁻¹ above the products.
The products are 50 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants; the peak is 45 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants.
The products are 45 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants; the peak is 95 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants.
pp.exp: Positive ΔH: products 45 kJ above reactants. The peak is 50 kJ above the reactants, which is just 5 kJ above the products.

pp.skill: Enthalpy change of neutralisation from a temperature rise
pp.mis: Using the volume of only one solution
pp.stem: 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ KOH(aq) is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃(aq). The temperature rises by 1.35 °C. Take the specific heat capacity of the mixture as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and its density as 1.00 g cm⁻³. What is the enthalpy change per mole of KOH?
pp.exp: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 1.35 = 564 J. n(KOH) = 0.0500 × 0.200 = 0.0100 mol. ΔH = −564 / 0.0100 = −56 400 J mol⁻¹ = −56.4 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because the temperature rose).

wrong.D: unit slip: the value is in kJ, not J

pp.skill: Neutralisation with a diprotic acid
pp.mis: Dividing by the moles of acid instead of moles of water formed
pp.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ is added to 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ KOH, both at the same starting temperature. The temperature rises by 10.5 °C. Assume all the energy heats the mixture, whose heat capacity is 4.2 J cm⁻³ K⁻¹. What is the enthalpy change of neutralisation (per mole of water formed)?
pp.exp: Energy = 125 × 4.2 × 10.5 = 5513 J. n(KOH) = 0.100 mol; n(H⁺) = 2 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol, so 0.100 mol of water forms. ΔH<sub>neut</sub> = −5513 / 0.100 = −55.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

wrong.B: used only the 100 cm³ of KOH
wrong.D: divided by the moles of H₂SO₄ (0.0500)

pp.skill: Setting up the calculation for ΔH of neutralisation
pp.mis: Using the wrong number of moles of water
pp.stem: 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃ is mixed with 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol dm⁻³ NaOH in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 10.0 °C. The specific heat capacity of the solution is 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Which expression gives ΔH<sub>neut</sub> in J mol⁻¹?
pp.exp: Total mass ≈ 80 g, so q = 80 × 4.2 × 10.0. Water formed = n(HNO₃) = 0.040 × 1.50 = 0.060 mol (not 0.12: each H⁺ meets one OH⁻).

pp.skill: Heat capacity per unit volume in a neutralisation
pp.mis: Doubling the moles because two solutions are mixed
pp.stem: 25 cm³ of solution containing 0.050 mol of HCl is mixed with 25 cm³ of solution containing 0.050 mol of KOH. The temperature rises by 13.4 K. The heat capacity per unit volume of the solution is 4.2 J K⁻¹ cm⁻³. Which expression gives the enthalpy change of neutralisation, in J mol⁻¹?

pp.skill: Enthalpy of combustion from a spirit-burner experiment
pp.mis: Dividing by the mass of fuel instead of the moles
pp.stem: A spirit burner containing propan-1-ol (M<sub>r</sub> 60) heats 150 cm³ of water in a copper can. The temperature of the water rises from 20.0 °C to 42.5 °C and 0.42 g of propan-1-ol is burned. Use c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What value of ΔH<sub>c</sub> is obtained (3 s.f.)?
pp.exp: q = 150 × 4.18 × 22.5 = 14 100 J. n = 0.42 / 60 = 0.0070 mol. ΔH<sub>c</sub> = −14.1 / 0.0070 = −2020 kJ mol⁻¹ (the data-book value is larger because heat is lost).

wrong.A: this is q in kJ, not per mole
wrong.B: divided by the mass in grams instead of moles

pp.skill: Mass of fuel needed when heat transfer is not 100%
pp.mis: Applying the efficiency in the wrong direction
pp.stem: A propane camping stove heats 500 g of water from 20 °C to 80 °C. Only 60% of the heat released by the burning propane reaches the water. ΔH<sub>c</sub>(propane) = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹; M<sub>r</sub>(C₃H₈) = 44; c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the minimum mass of propane that must be burned?
pp.exp: Heat needed by water = 500 × 4.18 × 60 = 125 400 J. Heat that must be released = 125 400 / 0.60 = 209 000 J = 209 kJ. n = 209 / 2220 = 0.0941 mol; mass = 0.0941 × 44 = 4.14 g.

pp.skill: Expressing ΔH using a single type of data
pp.mis: Forgetting that ΔH<sub>f</sub> of an element is zero
pp.stem:
2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g)
Which expression gives the standard enthalpy change of this reaction?
pp.exp: The equation is the combustion of 2 mol of CO, so ΔH = 2ΔH<sub>c</sub>(CO). (Using formation data it would be 2ΔH<sub>f</sub>(CO₂) − 2ΔH<sub>f</sub>(CO), which is not an option.)

pp.skill: Choosing a valid expression from combustion data
pp.mis: Using bond energies for a reaction involving liquids
pp.stem:
C₂H₅OH(l) → C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l)
Which expression gives ΔH for this reaction?
pp.exp: With combustion data, ΔH = Σ ΔH<sub>c</sub>(reactants) − Σ ΔH<sub>c</sub>(products). Water does not burn (ΔH<sub>c</sub> = 0). Bond energies apply to gases only, and D also ignores the C–H bond broken and the second O–H bond formed.

pp.skill: Hess’s law using enthalpies of combustion
pp.mis: Using products − reactants with combustion data
pp.stem: Ethene reacts with steam to form ethanol: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l) → C₂H₅OH(l). ΔH<sub>c</sub>(C₂H₄) = −1411 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH<sub>c</sub>(C₂H₅OH) = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?
pp.exp: ΔH = ΔH<sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΔH<sub>c</sub>(products) = (−1411 + 0) − (−1367) = −44 kJ mol⁻¹.

pp.skill: ΔH<sub>f</sub> from enthalpies of combustion
pp.mis: Not multiplying by the coefficients
pp.stem: ΔH<sub>c</sub> values / kJ mol⁻¹: C(s) −394, H₂(g) −286, C₂H₅OH(l) −1367. What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol?

pp.skill: ΔH<sub>c</sub> of a fuel from ΔH<sub>f</sub> and element combustion data
pp.mis: Adding ΔH<sub>f</sub> instead of subtracting it
pp.stem: ΔH<sub>c</sub>(C) = −394 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH<sub>c</sub>(H₂) = −286 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH<sub>f</sub>(C₃H₈) = −105 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the standard enthalpy change of combustion of propane?
pp.exp: Route via the elements: C₃H₈ → 3C + 4H₂ (+105), then burn them: 3(−394) + 4(−286) = −2326. Total = +105 − 2326 = −2221 kJ mol⁻¹.

pp.skill: ΔH<sub>r</sub> from enthalpies of formation
pp.mis: Forgetting the stoichiometric coefficients
pp.stem:
4NH₃(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2N₂(g) + 6H₂O(g)
ΔHf / kJ mol⁻¹: NH₃(g) −46.1; H₂O(g) −241.8. What is ΔH⦵ for this reaction?
pp.exp: ΔH = ΣΔH<sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔH<sub>f</sub>(reactants) = 6(−241.8) − 4(−46.1) = −1450.8 + 184.4 = −1266.4 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH<sub>f</sub> of N₂ and O₂ is zero.

pp.skill: Hess’s law with formation data for an acid
pp.mis: Adding all the formation values
pp.stem:
SO₃(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₄(l)
ΔHf / kJ mol⁻¹: SO₃(g) −396; H₂O(l) −286; H₂SO₄(l) −814. What is ΔH⦵?

pp.skill: Disproportionation enthalpy from formation data
pp.mis: Ignoring the element formed as a product
pp.stem: ΔH<sub>f</sub>(FeCl₂(s)) = −342 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH<sub>f</sub>(FeCl₃(s)) = −399 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy change for 3FeCl₂(s) → 2FeCl₃(s) + Fe(s)?
pp.exp: ΔH = 2(−399) + 0 − 3(−342) = −798 + 1026 = +228 kJ mol⁻¹. Fe(s) is an element, so its ΔH<sub>f</sub> is 0.

pp.skill: Combining formation data for an oxidation step
pp.mis: Not doubling for 2 mol
pp.stem: ΔH<sub>f</sub>(CO(g)) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH<sub>f</sub>(CO₂(g)) = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH<sup>⦵</sup> for 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g)?

pp.skill: Combining two thermochemical equations
pp.mis: Adding when one equation must be reversed
pp.stem:
N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g) ΔH = +180.6 kJ mol⁻¹
N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) ΔH = +66.4 kJ mol⁻¹
What is ΔH for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g)?
pp.exp: Reverse the first equation (−180.6) and add the second (+66.4): ΔH = −180.6 + 66.4 = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

pp.skill: ΔH<sub>f</sub> from a two-step route
pp.mis: Halving or doubling at the wrong step
pp.stem:
S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g) ΔH = −297 kJ mol⁻¹
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) ΔH = −196 kJ mol⁻¹
What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of SO₃(g)?
pp.exp: S(s) + 1½O₂(g) → SO₃(g) = (S → SO₂) + ½(2SO₂ → 2SO₃) = −297 + (−98) = −395 kJ mol⁻¹.

pp.skill: Reading an energy cycle
pp.mis: Going against the direction of an arrow without changing its sign
pp.stem: In an energy cycle, ΔH₁ is for C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₂ is for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g) and ΔH₃ is for CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g). Which expression equals ΔH₂?
pp.exp: Two routes from C + O₂ to CO₂: direct (ΔH₁) or via CO (ΔH₂ + ΔH₃). Hess’s law: ΔH₁ = ΔH₂ + ΔH₃, so ΔH₂ = ΔH₁ − ΔH₃.

pp.skill: Identifying formation reactions within a cycle
pp.mis: Including combustions of compounds
pp.stem:
Five reactions are listed.
1 C(s) + 2H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → CH₃OH(l)
2 C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
3 H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l)
4 CH₃OH(l) + 1½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
5 CO(g) + 2H₂(g) → CH₃OH(l)
For which reactions is ΔH⦵ an enthalpy change of formation?
pp.exp: Reactions 1, 2 and 3 each make 1 mol of a compound from elements in their standard states. (2 and 3 are also ΔH<sub>c</sub> of carbon and of hydrogen.) Reaction 4 starts from a compound, and 5 uses CO, a compound.

pp.skill: ΔH from average bond energies
pp.mis: Forgetting a bond that is formed
pp.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: C=C 610, C–C 350, C–H 410, H–H 436. What is ΔH?
pp.exp: Broken: C=C (610) + H–H (436) = 1046. Formed: C–C (350) + 2 C–H (820) = 1170. ΔH = 1046 − 1170 = −124 kJ mol⁻¹. (The four original C–H bonds are unchanged.)

wrong.C: counted only one new C–H bond

pp.skill: Finding an unknown bond energy from ΔH
pp.mis: Using the wrong sign for ΔH
pp.stem: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) ΔH = −184 kJ mol⁻¹. E(H–H) = 436 kJ mol⁻¹; E(H–Cl) = 431 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the bond energy of Cl–Cl?

pp.skill: Unknown bond energy in a substitution reaction
pp.mis: Subtracting ΔH instead of adding
pp.stem: C₂H₆(g) + Cl₂(g) → C₂H₅Cl(g) + HCl(g) ΔH = −109 kJ mol⁻¹. Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–H 410, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is the C–Cl bond energy?

pp.skill: Unknown bond energy from a combustion
pp.mis: Not dividing by the number of bonds formed
pp.stem: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) ΔH = −802 kJ mol⁻¹. Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–H 413, O=O 496, O–H 463. What is the average C=O bond energy in CO₂?

wrong.D: forgot that CO₂ has two C=O bonds

pp.skill: Defining ΔH<sub>f</sub>, writing its equations and using Hess’s law
pp.stem:
Chromium can be extracted by heating chromium(III) oxide with aluminium (a thermite reaction).
Cr₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → 2Cr(s) + Al₂O₃(s)

parts.q: Define standard enthalpy change of formation.
ms: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements
under standard conditions (298 K, 101 kPa) with all substances in their standard states

parts.q: Write equations, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy changes of formation of Cr₂O₃(s) and Al₂O₃(s).
ΔH<sub>f</sub>(Cr₂O₃) = −1140 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH<sub>f</sub>(Al₂O₃) = −1676 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔH<sub>r</sub> for the thermite reaction.

pp.skill: Formation equation and Hess’s law calculation
pp.stem: Silicon dioxide reacts with hydrogen fluoride gas: SiO₂(s) + 4HF(g) → SiF₄(g) + 2H₂O(l)

parts.q: Write an equation, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of formation of HF(g).

parts.q: ΔH<sub>f</sub> / kJ mol⁻¹: SiO₂(s) −911; HF(g) −273; SiF₄(g) −1615; H₂O(l) −286. Calculate ΔH for the reaction.

pp.skill: Pathway diagram, calorimetry and an indirect Hess calculation
pp.stem:
Potassium carbonate and potassium hydrogencarbonate both react with hydrochloric acid.
reaction 1: K₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2KCl + H₂O + CO₂ ΔH₁
reaction 2: KHCO₃ + HCl → KCl + H₂O + CO₂ ΔH₂ = +22.0 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.q: Ethene reacts with chlorine: CH₂=CH₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₂ClCH₂Cl(l), ΔH<sub>r</sub> = −219 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH<sub>f</sub>(ethene) = +52.2 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔH<sub>f</sub> of 1,2-dichloroethane.
Cyclohexene is hydrogenated: C₆H₁₀(l) + H₂(g) → C₆H₁₂(l). ΔH<sub>c</sub> / kJ mol⁻¹: C₆H₁₀ −3752; H₂ −286; C₆H₁₂ −3920. Calculate ΔH for the hydrogenation.

pp.skill: Sketching an energy profile with a catalyst
pp.stem: In a catalytic converter, dinitrogen oxide reacts with carbon monoxide: N₂O(g) + CO(g) → N₂(g) + CO₂(g). ΔH = −365 kJ mol⁻¹ and E<sub>a</sub> = +188 kJ mol⁻¹.

ms: the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react

parts.q: Describe the energy profile for this reaction, showing ΔH and E<sub>a</sub>.
ms: products drawn well below reactants (by 365), ΔH arrow pointing down
a hump above the reactants with E<sub>a</sub> arrow (188) from the reactants up to the peak
